passage:
Monday. In the back of his rough notebook, Lokesh, ten, kept a list: Baljeet lent eraser (2 times). Me helped Baljeet with maps (1). Ritu owes me a pencil.
Wednesday. After the class clean-up, Sir handed out laddoos: three for Lokesh, "my best helper", and one for Baljeet. Lokesh's face went red. "That's not fair! Baljeet carried six chairs, I carried four. He should get more!" The class stared. Sir blinked. "Lokesh, it's a laddoo." "It's the rule," Lokesh said, and pushed one across the desk.
Saturday. Baljeet saw the list while copying homework. "You count everything?" Lokesh shrugged, cheeks hot. "Someone has to." Baljeet laughed and crossed out "eraser (2)". "Keep your list. I don't need a bill."

qa.q: How many chairs did Baljeet carry, according to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh said Baljeet carried six chairs and Lokesh carried four.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's face go red when he got three laddoos?
qa.a: He felt upset that the split was unfair by his count, since Baljeet had worked harder, even though he was the one getting extra.

qa.q: Lokesh pushed a laddoo across. What could he try next time a split feels wrong?
qa.a: He could raise it quietly with Sir instead of shouting it in front of the class, keeping the fairness without the scene.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel on finding himself listed in Lokesh's notebook?
qa.a: Baljeet seems amused rather than hurt, and wants to show Lokesh that their friendship doesn't need keeping count.

grounding: Across a week, a child keeps a tally of favours and loudly objects to a split that favours himself, showing an early, rigid sense of fairness.

passage: Jomon, you're counting the chocolates again, I can see your lips moving. Come here, mone. When your Seema aunty was nine, I was worse. I kept a tally on the kitchen wall with charcoal: who pumped water, who fed the hens, who helped whom with sums. One day my father cut a jackfruit and gave me the biggest share because I had swept the yard. I shouted, "No! Thomas pumped water twice, he gets more!" Everyone laughed, and my father said, "Seema, just eat." I wouldn't touch it until Thomas had the bigger piece. I was right about fairness, mind you. But I was so busy counting that I never enjoyed a single bite. Share them, mone, and don't keep a wall.

qa.q: Where did young Seema keep her tally?
qa.a: On the kitchen wall, with charcoal.

qa.q: Why wouldn't young Seema touch her jackfruit?
qa.a: She felt the split was unfair because Thomas had pumped water twice, and she couldn't enjoy extra she felt she hadn't earned.

qa.q: What is Seema aunty hoping Jomon will choose with the chocolates?
qa.a: She hopes Jomon will share them freely rather than counting every piece, keeping fairness without letting the tally spoil the fun.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when young Seema shouted that he should get more?
qa.a: Thomas may have been surprised and a bit embarrassed by the fuss, but perhaps pleased that his work was noticed.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a child, she kept a tally of chores and refused a bigger share that was meant for her, fairness held rigidly.

passage: The school fair closed in five minutes, the lights were going off one by one, and the lemonade stall's tin was full of sticky coins. "Quick, just grab and go," said Pallavi, pushing a bigger heap towards Himani. "You made the sign." "No!" Himani's voice rang across the ground. "You squeezed forty lemons. I only squeezed twelve. And Mehak washed all the cups. We count it properly." The watchman was already rattling his keys at the gate. Pallavi groaned. Himani knelt on the grass, sorting coins by torchlight: one pile for squeezing, one for cups, one for the sign. Her own pile came out smallest. She nodded, satisfied, just as the gate clanged.

qa.q: How many lemons did Pallavi squeeze, according to Himani?
qa.a: Himani said Pallavi squeezed forty lemons.

qa.q: Why did Himani look satisfied even though her own pile came out smallest?
qa.a: What mattered to her was that each pile matched the work done; a fair count felt better than extra coins.

qa.q: With the gate closing, what could Himani have chosen instead of sorting every coin?
qa.a: She could have taken the tin home and split it properly next day, keeping fairness without keeping everyone waiting in the dark.

qa.q: What is it like for Pallavi to have a generous offer turned down so loudly?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel frustrated and a little embarrassed, since the bigger heap was meant kindly and she just wanted to go home.

grounding: A child insists loudly on an exact split of stall money by effort, even though it leaves her with less, showing a rigid sense of fairness.

passage: Minakshi, nine, and Hafsa washed Mr Kapoor's car every Sunday in their Lucknow colony. This Sunday, Mr Kapoor gave Minakshi sixty rupees and Hafsa forty. "For my neighbour's girl, a little extra," he winked. Minakshi's face went hot. "That's not fair! Hafsa did the wheels and the mats. I only did the windows. She should get more!" Mr Kapoor laughed. "It's only twenty rupees, beta." "It's the rule," Minakshi said, and pushed twenty rupees into Hafsa's hand. That night she opened her notebook. Every Sunday had a line: who did wheels, who did windows, who brought the bucket. Hafsa, reading over her shoulder, giggled. "You even wrote the bucket?" "Somebody has to keep it fair," Minakshi said, underlining it twice.

qa.q: How much money did Mr Kapoor first give Minakshi?
qa.a: He gave Minakshi sixty rupees.

qa.q: Why was Minakshi upset even though she got more money?
qa.a: She felt the split was unfair because Hafsa had done the wheels and the mats, which was more work than her windows.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's notebook do well, and where could it go too far?
qa.a: It helps her keep things fair, but counting even the bucket every week could turn a fun friendship into a strict account.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Minakshi's notebook?
qa.a: Hafsa finds it funny that her friend writes down even who brought the bucket, though she also benefits from Minakshi's sense of fairness.

grounding: A nine-year-old refuses an unequal payment in her favour and keeps a strict notebook of who did what, showing an emerging, rigid sense of fairness.

passage:
"Nani, you gave me thirty and Nikhil twenty." Ankita, ten, held up the coins.
"You fetched the vegetables, beti."
"But Nikhil fetched the milk twice and the newspaper. That's three trips. I only did one."
Nikhil, eight, looked up hopefully. "She's right, Nani."
"Arrey, it's just pocket money."
"It's not fair if it's not counted." Ankita took out a sheet of paper. "I'm making a chart. Trips, sweeping, watering plants. Each gets five rupees."
"And who checks the chart?" Nani asked, amused.
"Me."
"And if I give you extra because you're my first grandchild?"
"Then I'll give it to Nikhil." Ankita slid ten rupees across the table.
Nani shook her head, smiling. "This girl will run a bank one day."
Nikhil pocketed the coins before anyone could change their mind.

qa.q: What did Ankita fetch for Nani?
qa.a: She fetched the vegetables.

qa.q: What does Ankita's chart suggest about how she feels about fairness?
qa.a: It suggests she is determined that fairness means counting exactly, even when counting leaves her with less.

qa.q: How could Nani help Ankita keep fairness without making it rigid?
qa.a: She could praise Ankita's honesty and also explain that small gifts of love don't always need to be counted like payments.

qa.q: How does Nikhil see Ankita's rule?
qa.a: Nikhil is happy and a bit surprised, since Ankita's strict counting gives Nikhil more money.

grounding: A ten-year-old objects to an unequal split in her favour and makes a strict chart of chores, showing a strong but rigid sense of fairness.

passage:
Sunday
Today Mami cut the big mango for Ayesha and me. She gave me three slices and Ayesha only two. Ayesha didn't even notice. But I said, "That's not fair! Ayesha should get the same!" Mami laughed and said I was being funny. I wasn't. I kept thinking about it.
I also counted: Ayesha helped me with my kite on Friday, and I helped her with her maths on Saturday. So we're even. Last week Rahim from next door borrowed my bat twice and never lent me his cricket ball once. I have written that down.
Mami says I'm like a shopkeeper. But I think things should be equal. Otherwise it feels wrong in my tummy.
- Samir

qa.q: How many mango slices did Samir get?
qa.a: Samir got three slices.

qa.q: Why did Samir object to getting more mango?
qa.a: Samir felt it was unfair and uncomfortable, a wrong feeling in the tummy, because things should be equal even when Samir gets the extra.

qa.q: What could Mami say to help Samir think about fairness?
qa.a: Mami could praise Samir for caring about fairness, and gently explain that not every kindness needs to be counted exactly.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Samir's objection?
qa.a: Ayesha didn't even notice the unequal split, so she might be surprised Samir cared so much.

grounding: A child keeps score of favours and objects to an unequal split even when getting the extra, showing an emerging, rigid sense of fairness.

passage: At the temple fair in their village, Jyoti's uncle bought kulfi for the children and gave Keerthana, nine, two sticks and Jyoti only one. "Keerthana helped carry the water pots," he said. Keerthana frowned. "But Jyoti carried the flowers. That's the same work." She held out one kulfi to Jyoti. Jyoti shook her head. "Keep it, you like pista." Keerthana stamped her foot. "No! It has to be equal." Jyoti's uncle laughed. "Such a strict judge!" But Keerthana kept holding it out until Jyoti took it. Then she counted who had carried what at the fair all morning, on her fingers, just to be sure.

qa.q: How many kulfi sticks did Jyoti's uncle give Keerthana?
qa.a: He gave Keerthana two sticks.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: Keerthana felt upset and determined that the split was unfair, even though she was getting the extra.

qa.q: What could Jyoti's uncle say to help Keerthana relax a little about fairness?
qa.a: He could agree that fairness matters, and explain that sometimes a small extra is just a thank-you, not something to fight over.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel about Keerthana's strict fairness?
qa.a: Jyoti seemed amused and generous, happy to let Keerthana keep it, maybe a bit surprised by how much it mattered to her friend.

grounding: A child objects loudly to an unequal kulfi split even when she gets the extra, and keeps score of who did what, showing a rigid sense of fairness.

passage: In their Mexico City classroom, Camila, eleven, and her group got their project back: an A. The teacher said the group could split ten bonus stickers however they liked. Olga said, "Camila did the most. She should get four." Camila shook her head hard. "No, it should be even. Two each, and I have a list." She pulled out a notebook: who drew the map, who wrote the report, who brought glue. "Olga did the map. Ben did the cover." The others groaned. "You don't have to be so exact," Ben said. Camila's cheeks went pink. "But it's not fair if it's not fair." The teacher smiled. "Camila, you care a lot about fairness. That's good. Maybe fairness can have a little space for thank-yous too."

qa.q: How many bonus stickers could the group split?
qa.a: They could split ten bonus stickers.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when Ben said she didn't have to be so exact?
qa.a: Camila felt embarrassed and stubborn, cheeks going pink, sure that fairness mattered.

qa.q: What does the teacher's comment help Camila see?
qa.a: That caring about fairness is good, but fairness can also leave room for generosity and thank-yous.

qa.q: How might Olga have felt when Camila refused the extra stickers?
qa.a: Olga may have felt surprised and a little frustrated, since she was trying to thank Camila.

grounding: A child keeps a list of who helped and insists on equal shares even when offered the extra, showing a sometimes rigid sense of fairness.

passage:
At the school canteen, Aunty was scooping out rajma-chawal. Rukmini's plate got a huge heap because Aunty knew her mother. Rehana, next in line, got a small scoop because the pot was nearly empty.
"That's not fair!" Rukmini said loudly. "I got more than Rehana!"
"Eat, beta. Don't make a fuss."
"No! She helped me carry the sports mats this morning. She should get the same." Rukmini scraped half her rajma onto Rehana's plate, spilling some.
The boys in the line laughed. Rehana went pink. "It's okay, Rukmini. Really."
"It's not okay. Equal is equal." Rukmini crossed her arms and wouldn't eat till the plates looked the same.

qa.q: What was Aunty scooping out at the canteen?
qa.a: She was scooping out rajma-chawal.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini make a fuss even though she got more?
qa.a: She felt strongly that it was unfair, and remembered that Rehana had helped her, so the unequal split upset her.

qa.q: What went well and what went a bit too far?
qa.a: Caring about fairness was good, but insisting loudly and scraping food across plates embarrassed Rehana; she could have quietly offered to share.

qa.q: How does Rehana seem to feel when Rukmini scrapes rajma onto her plate?
qa.a: Rehana feels embarrassed, going pink as the boys laugh, even though she knows Rukmini means well.

grounding: Shows a child who remembers a classmate's help objecting loudly to an unequal split even though she got the extra, a sense of fairness applied rigidly.

passage:
Monday: Sangeeta wrote in her notebook: "I washed dishes. Tanvir did NOT." She drew a big cross next to her brother's name.
Wednesday: Mummy gave Sangeeta the bigger slice of birthday cake because it was her birthday. "No," said Sangeeta, "Tanvir helped decorate. Cut it again." Mummy sighed and cut two careful halves with a ruler.
Saturday: Tanvir swept the balcony without being asked. Sangeeta checked her notebook and wrote: "Tanvir swept. So he gets the window seat on the bus." Then she frowned. "But he didn't dry the dishes on Monday." Tanvir groaned. "Do you count everything?"
"Somebody has to," she said.

qa.q: Why did Mummy give Sangeeta the bigger slice?
qa.a: Because it was her birthday.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta refuse the bigger slice on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt indignant that the split was unfair, because Tanvir had helped decorate, and her sense of fairness mattered more than extra cake.

qa.q: What could help Sangeeta keep her fairness without counting everything?
qa.a: Mummy could praise her fairness and suggest that small differences even out over time, so not every favour needs a note.

qa.q: How does Tanvir seem to feel about the notebook by Saturday?
qa.a: Tanvir feels frustrated and tired of being counted, groaning when Sangeeta brings up Monday's dishes.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a record of who helped and objecting to an unequal split even when she would get the extra, over several days.

passage:
Nazia, you want to count every chocolate your cousin gets? Let your Dadu tell you about his notebook. I'm Vijay, and when I was ten, I kept a little green notebook.
In it I wrote everything. "Ravi lent me his pencil. I owe Ravi." "Mother gave Suresh two ladoos and me three. Wrong!" I even gave back one ladoo, and my mother laughed so much she had to sit down.
I thought I was being fair. But I once refused to play with my best friend for a whole week because he'd forgotten to return a marble.
My father read the notebook and said, "Vijay, keep caring about fairness. But friends aren't a shop."

qa.q: What colour was Vijay's notebook?
qa.a: The notebook was green.

qa.q: Why did young Vijay give back one ladoo?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair that he got more than Suresh, and his strong sense of fairness made him want an equal split.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have been different?
qa.a: Refusing to play with his best friend for a week over a marble; he could have reminded the friend and kept playing.

qa.q: How might the best friend have felt that week?
qa.a: The friend likely felt hurt and confused, losing a playmate over one forgotten marble.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a child keeping score of favours and objecting to unequal splits even when he got the extra, sometimes too rigidly.

passage: The power went out halfway through decorating the building's Navratri stage, and there were only two hours left before garba. By torchlight, Nirmala Aunty handed out the leftover pedas. "Ankita, four for you. You worked hardest." "No!" Ankita's voice rang across the dark courtyard. "That's not fair. The twins carried the chairs. The Joshi boy tied every marigold string. I only held the ladder." "Beta, it's just pedas." "It's not just pedas. Everyone gets three, or I don't want mine." A few adults laughed. Nirmala Aunty sighed and split them again, three each, while the torch flickered. Ankita counted carefully, then nodded, satisfied.

qa.q: How many pedas did Nirmala Aunty first give Ankita?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: Why was Ankita so upset about getting extra?
qa.a: She felt indignant because others had worked as hard or harder; fairness mattered to her more than getting more.

qa.q: What could Ankita try next time she feels something is unfair?
qa.a: She could say it calmly and privately to Aunty, which would still make her point without the whole courtyard hearing.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty see Ankita's outburst?
qa.a: She might feel a little embarrassed and tired in the rush, but also see that Ankita cares deeply about fairness.

grounding: Shows a child keeping track of who helped and objecting loudly to an unequal split even when she would get more.

passage: New Year's Eve in the flat, with fairy lights taped along the window. Papa cut the chocolate cake and slid the biggest slice to Sudha. "For my helper." Sudha pushed it back. "No, Papa. Shankar carried all the chairs up from Mrs Pinto's flat. I only folded napkins." Shankar looked up, surprised. Sudha pulled a small notebook from her pocket. "I wrote it down. Monday, I dried dishes. Tuesday, Shankar watered plants. Today, chairs." Papa laughed. "You keep a register?" "Somebody has to," said Sudha seriously. "Equal slices." Papa cut again, carefully. Shankar grinned and whispered, "Thanks."

qa.q: What did Sudha pull from her pocket?
qa.a: A small notebook.

qa.q: What does Sudha's notebook suggest about how she thinks?
qa.a: It suggests she cares a lot, maybe a bit rigidly, about fairness; she feels uncomfortable taking more than her share and keeps careful track.

qa.q: How could Papa respond to Sudha's register in a helpful way?
qa.a: He could praise her fairness while gently saying that small kindnesses don't always need to be counted.

qa.q: How does Shankar see his sister's protest?
qa.a: He is surprised and grateful, glad she noticed his work with the chairs.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping score of favours and objecting to an unequal split that favours her.

passage: "Eid Mubarak! Sevaiyan for everyone!" Ammi set the bowls down. "Zainab, the big bowl is yours." "Why mine?" "You helped me roast the vermicelli." "Imran peeled all the almonds. That took forever." Imran looked up from his phone. "It's fine, take it." "It's not fine." Zainab crossed her arms. "Last Eid you got the big bowl because you went to the market. So this time it should be equal, or you should have it." "You remember last Eid?" Ammi asked. "Of course I do." Imran laughed. "She's like a bank." Ammi poured some from the big bowl into Imran's. "Happy now, little judge?" Zainab checked both bowls. "Now it's fair."

qa.q: What did Imran peel?
qa.a: All the almonds.

qa.q: How can you tell Zainab feels strongly about fairness?
qa.a: She crosses her arms, refuses the big bowl, and remembers who got more last Eid; she feels uneasy until the bowls are equal.

qa.q: What would you advise Zainab about keeping score?
qa.a: Caring about fairness is good, but she could let small things go sometimes, since families even out over many Eids.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when his sister insists on equal bowls?
qa.a: He finds it funny, calling her a bank, but probably also feels noticed for peeling the almonds.

grounding: Shows a child tracking who did what across festivals and objecting to getting the larger share.

passage: Last Eid, when I was nine, I kept a list in my head all day. Simran had carried the plates. I had stirred the seviyan. Our cousin Ayaan had done nothing except eat raisins. When Khala handed out the nankhatai biscuits, she gave me five and Simran three, because I'd been in the kitchen longest. I should have been happy. Instead I shouted, "That's not FAIR! Four and four!" Everyone stared. Khala laughed. "Zainab, you're complaining about getting MORE?" I was. It felt wrong in my tummy. Then I told Khala that Ayaan should get only one because he did nothing, and nobody laughed at that. Now I think fair is a bit more wobbly than I thought.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Khala give Simran?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Zainab shout "That's not FAIR" about getting more?
qa.a: Zainab felt uncomfortable and upset, with a wrong feeling in the tummy, because an unequal split seemed unfair even with the extra coming to Zainab.

qa.q: What could Khala say to help Zainab think about fairness?
qa.a: Khala could praise Zainab's care for fairness and talk gently about how sharing can be kind, not only exact, so Ayaan isn't cut down to one biscuit.

qa.q: How might Ayaan feel about Zainab's one-biscuit idea?
qa.a: Ayaan might feel hurt and left out, since eating raisins at a festival hardly seems a crime to a small cousin.

grounding: A child keeps score of who helped and objects loudly to an unequal split even when receiving the extra.
